reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.81 and the ERA projection at 3.39, and that gap is almost entirely noise between an elite skill set and the randomness of run prevention over a full season. Skenes misses bats at a 30.4% clip while walking just 5.7% of hitters, a combination that makes contact management almost secondary, and his 33.8% chase rate explains why the strikeouts aren't just a function of hitters expanding early in counts. The one thing worth watching is that his whiff rate runs closer to average than the rest of the profile suggests it should, which means the 230 projected strikeouts lean heavily on hitters chasing out of the zone rather than getting beaten on swings at good pitches. If that chase rate softens, he's still a sub-3.40 ERA arm over a heavy workload; if it holds, you're looking at a genuine frontline ace at 23.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

At 92.9 mph average exit velocity and 52.2% hard-hit rate, he's doing elite contact damage, and the 30.3 ft/s sprint speed converts a portion of that damage that would retire anyone else. The one friction point is a 33.0% chase rate, which suppresses his walk opportunities and is the reason the OBP projection stays at .351 despite the raw contact ability; if that rate tightens even modestly, the offensive profile takes a significant step up. reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The gap between what Nick Kurtz hits and how often he misses is the whole tension in this profile. His 93.6 mph average exit velocity and 18.1% barrel rate both sit at the 97th percentile, and his 18.3% walk rate is among the best in baseball — but a 36.8% whiff rate at the 2nd percentile means pitchers have found the zone to attack, and a 32.2% strikeout rate bleeds away the contact that his xwOBA of .375 suggests he's capable of. The projection (.891 OPS, 33 home runs) hinges entirely on whether he can trim enough of those whiffs to let the elite contact quality and elite plate discipline work together rather than against each other. If he does, he's an All-Star-caliber first baseman; if the strikeouts stay where they are, he's a fascinating, frustrating power source who leaves runs on the table.

The hard-hit rate of 44.2% is the one legitimate counter, he does punish mistakes, but it isn't converting into the kind of expected production that justifies a franchise-shortstop ceiling. reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report:
A 4.4% strikeout rate is not a misprint. Arraez makes contact at a level that has no real peer in the current game, and his 7.8% whiff rate backs up every bit of it, the projection's .317 AVG in 682 PA following directly from that contact quality being fully sustainable.

The tension is that the bat-to-ball skill and the raw power are almost comically mismatched: a 0.5% barrel rate, 21.0% hard-hit rate, and 87.0 mph average exit velocity sitting near the bottom of the league. His xSLG is .371 and his xwOBA .304, meaning the contact he makes is soft by design, and the projection's .432 SLG depends heavily on his speed and placement keeping the slugging inflated past what the quality of contact would ordinarily support.

What he is: a second-division regular if the batting average stays up and the legs stay fresh, a below-average regular if either slips, because there is no power floor to catch him.

reports.name: Randy Arozarena
reports.published_report: The .352 xwOBA and 91.0 mph average exit velocity tell the same story: Arozarena makes loud contact more consistently than his barrel rate suggests, because he hits the ball hard across a wide range of launch conditions rather than depending on one perfect swing plane. The profile hinge is the 31.7% chase rate, which feeds a 28.1% whiff rate — if pitchers keep him from settling into a comfortable zone, the strikeout numbers climb and the walk rate that currently sits at 9.7% starts to erode with it. If the discipline holds, 19 home runs and 27 stolen bases in 648 projected plate appearances sketches a genuinely well-rounded outfielder, a multi-category regular who contributes without dominating any single dimension. Take away the speed or let the chase rate spike, and what remains is a useful, slightly below-average defensive corner piece hitting for solid average.

reports.name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are genuinely alarming: a 7th-percentile xBA and a 31.5% whiff rate that drag the whole Statcast batting profile down into the bottom fifth of the league. Everything else on the card is at least serviceable, 90.8 mph average exit velo, a 9.6% walk rate, elite defense, but the swing-and-miss is severe enough that the projection lands at .226/.302/.418 across 602 PA, which is a below-average offensive line even with 26 home runs and 39 stolen bases baked in. The speed and raw power are loud, and the 97th-percentile OAA makes him genuinely valuable on both sides of the ball. This whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten contact rates enough to stop giving the power back at the plate; if the whiff rate stays where it is, you're looking at a high-variance, below-average regular whose counting stats flatter a weak batting line.

reports.name: Isaac Paredes
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is genuinely strange for a guy projected at 23 home runs. His 16.5% whiff rate sits in the 91st percentile, and his 15.0% strikeout rate is well below the league norm, yet his 86.7 mph average exit velocity ranks in just the 14th percentile and his 30.1% hard-hit rate is near the bottom of the league. He makes consistent contact, then does almost nothing with it when he does make it. What keeps the power projection credible is plate discipline: a 9.5% walk rate and a 27.4% chase rate work together to give him enough at-bats to accumulate damage despite the soft contact, and the .257/.352/.436 projection reflects exactly that, a patient hitter who earns his runs the slow way. If the walk rate erodes and pitchers stop throwing him strikes he has to take, the .436 SLG evaporates quickly, because there's no exit-velocity floor to catch him.

reports.name: Ceddanne Rafaela
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely red except for two things, and those two things are why he's rostered everywhere. Rafaela's sprint speed at 29.1 ft/s and his OAA grade sit at the elite end of the spectrum, but everything underneath the contact tells a harder story: an xwOBA of .281 at the 9th percentile, exit velocity at 86.3 mph, and a 41.7% chase rate that only 4% of hitters run worse. The projection's .270/.313/.429 line leans on BABIP-friendly speed converting weak contact into hits at a rate the underlying quality can't really sustain, and if pitchers keep attacking him aggressively outside the zone, the .313 OBP and 4.4% walk rate both get worse before they get better. What you're buying is a 17-homer, 21-steal profile from a plus-plus defender in center, which is genuinely useful — just understand the bat is the floor, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 38.7% chase rate isn't a curiosity — it's the engine. Sánchez gets hitters to chase out of the zone at a rate that sits at the 99th percentile, and he pairs it with a 4.5% walk rate that's essentially unreachable for most starters, meaning he can live on the edges all game without self-destructing. The 32.4% whiff rate confirms hitters aren't just chasing and fouling off; they're missing, which is why 222 projected strikeouts over 202.8 innings feels grounded in the actual shape of his stuff. The one real tension in the profile is hard contact: a 43.8% hard-hit rate and 89.6 mph average exit velocity point to a pitcher who can be hurt when hitters do connect, so a 2.75 ERA projection over a full season depends on the chase and whiff numbers holding up against a full year of lineups.

A 48.5% strikeout rate with a 9.2% walk rate is the tension in the profile: the whiffs are historic, the command is the one thing keeping this from being a perfect closer season.

His 47.7% whiff rate and a 37.5% chase rate explain why contact, when it happens, is this weak. Hitters are so far behind or outside the zone that 84.8 mph average exit velocity is what you get, the xwOBA sits at .182 and the xERA at 1.41, and that isn't a favorable-conditions story. It's what happens when barrels are at 2.9% and hard contact at 25.0%.

The projection carries that forward: 37 saves, a 1.31 ERA, and 119 strikeouts across 66.6 innings, riding a 101.3 mph fastball at 2534 rpm that batters simply aren't catching up to. If the walk rate creeps past 9.2%, if the command erodes under a heavier workload or after an injury, you still have a dominant strikeout arm, just one living closer to the edge of counts than the rest of this Statcast card suggests.

reports.name: Cade Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout profile is elite and the contact profile is a problem — that tension is the whole read on Cade Smith. His K% sits at 34.7 and his whiff rate at 34.1%, both historically good numbers, but when contact does land, it lands hard: 44.6% hard-hit rate with an average exit velocity of 92.0 mph, the kind of contact suppression numbers that make you nervous about the ERA holding. The xERA of 3.22 and xwOBA of .279 suggest the actual 2.74 ERA gets some regression eventually, but a 5.7% walk rate keeps him from beating himself, and 41 projected saves says Cleveland trusts him to close regardless.

reports.published_report: The OBP is what this profile is actually built on. The 5.3% barrel rate and 38.9% hard-hit rate explain why the power projection lands at 18 home runs rather than anything more; he squares balls up infrequently enough that the .389 xSLG is probably close to his ceiling, not a floor. reports.name: Bryan Woo
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine here: 5.1% puts Woo in the 95th percentile, and when you pair that kind of control with a 34.7% chase rate, you can pitch aggressively to contact without paying a steep price. The hard-hit numbers are loud at 43.1%, and the 24.6% whiff rate sits right around average, so this isn't a swing-and-miss profile keeping hitters off balance. What keeps it from falling apart is the .291 xwOBA and 3.52 xERA, which say he's been genuinely effective even if the strikeout volume is modest, and that holds as long as the zone control stays elite. If the walk rate creeps toward ordinary, the contact quality becomes a real problem instead of a manageable one. A mid-rotation starter who profiles closer to his xERA than his ERA if the command holds.

A 37.2% chase rate and 30.2% whiff rate sit at the bottom of the league, and the projection's .313 OBP reflects exactly that ceiling — he's leaving real value on the table every time he expands the zone. reports.name: Wilyer Abreu
reports.published_report: The xSLG of .468 with a 12.6% barrel rate is the spine of this profile, both sitting in the 83rd percentile, and together they explain why the projected .441 slugging carries weight across a full 663 plate appearances. The average exit velocity at 89.8 mph lands only around the middle of the field, so the damage comes from barrel efficiency rather than raw thunder — he finds the sweet spot more reliably than he hits it hardest. A 9.6% walk rate and a 31.5% chase rate that grades below-average aggression round out a profile that is patient enough to post a .326 OBP without leaning on average. If the 92nd-percentile OAA holds in the outfield, Abreu is a solid everyday contributor whose value stacks on both sides of the ball; if the barrel rate softens toward what the hard-hit numbers suggest, you're looking at a good-glove second-division regular with modest offensive upside.

reports.name: Jeremy Peña
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .304 in the 99th percentile, yet his average exit velocity is 88.1 mph and his barrel rate is 4.9%. That's the whole profile in miniature: Peña makes an implausible amount of contact quality out of ordinary raw power, which is why the .293 projection AVG is believable even though the exit-velo numbers look pedestrian. Add 29.2 ft/s sprint speed and a 16.3% strikeout rate, and you have a shortstop who gets on base through contact efficiency and creates value on the bases rather than in the barrel. The risk is entirely contact-dependent — if the batted-ball luck regresses toward what the 88.1 mph exit velo suggests it should, the .802 OPS projection erodes fast, and what's left is a serviceable everyday shortstop rather than a plus one.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is eye-catching enough on its own, but the combination is what's loud here. Across A+ & A in 2026, Seth Hernandez has struck out 118 batters in 74 innings, a 14.3 K/9 that translates to 9.5 at the MLB level, and the 30% K-BB% sits at the 99th percentile of his pitcher pool while a 2.4 ERA and 1.1 WHIP push both run-prevention metrics to the 94th. The translation does soften the walk rate, 3.8 BB/9 here becoming 4.0 in MLB terms, where the average arm is sitting at 3.2, and that's the profile's hinge: if the command tightens as he climbs, you get a back-end starter; if the walks hold at that translated rate into Double-A and beyond, the floor is a depth arm.

reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The contact-quality profile here is almost absurdly good, with a 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 19.7% barrel rate, and then you hit the 42.9% whiff rate and the whole thing gets complicated. He makes rare, elite contact when he connects, and an 18.4% walk rate means he earns his base on balls when pitchers try to work around him. But a 33.0% strikeout rate against that whiff number says MLB arms are still finding the holes, and the projection's .228 AVG reflects exactly that tension: the underlying power translates to 34 home runs over 540 PA, but the batting average is the cost. The profile hinges entirely on whether the contact rate stabilizes even a little, because if it does, the xSLG of .502 becomes real damage, and if it doesn't, he's a high-strikeout slugger you can pitch around, a second-division regular carrying the load at first base for a White Sox team that doesn't have many other threats.

A legitimate second-division regular if the speed and contact hold; a fringe bench piece if pitchers start attacking the zone and his exit velocity has nowhere to go.

His chase rate at 31.4% is genuinely useful, hitters are expanding out of the zone, but his whiff rate at 23.7% means they're not missing once they chase, and the barrel rate at 10.6% is the part that should concern you most. If the contact quality stays that punishing, the projection ERA is doing him a favor he hasn't earned yet on the Statcast sheet. The optimistic read is that 114.5 innings with a 3.51 ERA looks like a real mid-rotation contributor; the honest read is that he's one bad stretch of hard contact away from looking like a back-end arm who got lucky on sequencing.

reports.name: A.J. Ewing
reports.published_report: The legs and the bat are pulling in opposite directions, and that tension is the whole profile. Ewing's 29.5 ft/s sprint speed lands in the 95th percentile, which explains the 20 projected steals and gives him a baserunning dimension that most outfielders can't match, but a 26.9% strikeout rate undercuts everything contact-dependent in the line. The contact quality reads as quietly ordinary, .320 xwOBA and a 6.7% barrel rate, enough to project a .260/.331/.393 slash across 436 plate appearances, which is a second-division regular if the speed and a solid OAA profile in the outfield carry their weight. If the strikeout rate creeps further, the floor is a bench outfielder whose speed shows up in late-game situations and not much else.

reports.name: Foster Griffin
reports.published_report: The projection and the Statcast card are telling two different stories, and that gap is what you have to reckon with here. ValuCast sees 186.6 innings at a 3.09 ERA with a 1.10 WHIP; the current Statcast profile shows a 3.92 xERA and a .306 xwOBA, both sitting right around average. What's keeping him on the field and keeping rallies quiet isn't swing-and-miss, it's location: a 5.6% walk rate lands in the 90th percentile, and a 33.4% chase rate is genuinely above average, so hitters are either expanding or waiting for walks that rarely come. The fastball is a liability at 91.4 mph with 2092 rpm spin, both near the bottom of the league, which is why the strikeout rate at 22.6% is middling, and if his command slips even modestly, that fastball has nowhere to hide. The projection is banking on him running a heavy workload with control as the engine, and the Statcast data says the engine works right now, but it has almost no margin for error.

reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 257 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The .338 average at AAA is the loudest thing in this profile, and it deserves some skepticism before you start booking flights to Coors. A .387 BABIP is doing meaningful work there, and the 30 stolen bases in 257 plate appearances signal that the hit-tool reads are getting help from legs, too. What survives the translation is still interesting: a 15% strikeout rate at AAA becomes 18.9% against MLB pitching, where the league strikes out at 22.0%, and the walk rate translates to 9.2% with the MLB average sitting at 8.5%, so the plate discipline is credible and not a product of the level. The ISO at .191 in AAA becomes .152 in MLB-equivalent terms, essentially league-average pop, which tells you the ceiling here is a low-end everyday center fielder if the contact and speed translate, and a reserve piece if the BABIP comes back to earth and the bat can't carry without it.

reports.name: Trea Turner
reports.published_report: The sprint speed still shows up at 29.8 ft/s, 98th percentile, and that number alone keeps him relevant in any lineup conversation. But the bat that used to justify a cornerstone role has quietly become a problem: his xwOBA sits at .295, his chase rate is 35.0%, and a 6.2% walk rate gives him almost no margin for error when pitchers find the edges. A .303 OBP built on a .251 average is a fragile structure, and it collapses if the contact erodes any further. What he is now is a high-volume speed contributor whose ceiling depends entirely on whether he can stop expanding the zone enough to let that average climb back toward what 29.8 ft/s deserves.

reports.name: Kyle Schwarber
reports.published_report: 48 home runs projected from a bat with an 18.3% barrel rate and a 34.7% strikeout rate — that's the whole profile in two numbers, pointing in opposite directions. When he makes contact, the ball does damage at a level almost no hitter in baseball replicates: 93.3 mph average exit velocity, 52.0% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .503 that his projected .527 SLG actually believes. The strikeouts are the cost of doing business, not a warning sign, because his 13.9% walk rate keeps the .358 OBP livable and the lineup spot honest. If the contact rate erodes further, the OBP floor goes with it, and the profile thins fast, but at full health across 691 plate appearances, this is a middle-of-the-order bat with one gear.

reports.name: Andre Pallante
reports.published_report: Contact management is the whole bet here. Pallante's 17.7% strikeout rate is among the lowest in the league, and his 21.1% whiff rate isn't generating the swings-and-misses that typically sustain a rotation spot, but hitters aren't doing damage when they do connect: a 5.8% barrel rate and 33.9% hard-hit rate both sit comfortably below the field. The walk rate of 6.8% is his quiet asset, throwing strikes and keeping runners off base while letting the contact-suppression shape carry a 3.65 xERA without missing bats. If that contact suppression softens and hitters start squaring him up at a league-average clip, there's no strikeout floor to catch him, and the 163.8-inning workhorse picture collapses into a backend arm fighting to hold a rotation spot.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile is almost uniformly bad, and the projection asks you to believe it gets meaningfully better. A 5.47 xERA and 16.3% strikeout rate from current MLB exposure represent a pitcher who misses almost no bats, 18.7% whiff rate puts him near the bottom of the league, and hitters are squaring him up at a 42.2% hard-hit rate. The one genuine asset is a 5.9% walk rate, which keeps counts manageable but can't compensate for a profile this light on swing-and-miss.

ValuCast's 3.48 ERA projection over 180.7 innings is carrying real optimism that contact quality will regress toward him, and the entire profile hinges on whether that regression arrives, because if the 16.3% strikeout rate is who he actually is at 91.7 mph, the floor here is a back-end arm leaking runs. Either a useful innings-eater whose contact management clicks, or a league-average ERA is a ceiling he can't reach.

reports.name: Sean Burke
reports.published_report: The fastball spin is the whole profile: 2582 rpm ranks in the 96th percentile, and it explains how a 94.9 mph heater punches up a 27.0% strikeout rate without elite swing-and-miss numbers. His 25.2% Whiff % is right at the middle of the pack, yet hitters are chasing at 33.0% and getting to hard contact less than you'd expect given the velocity. The xERA sits at 3.44, and ValuCast projects him for a 3.58 ERA over 174.2 innings, which on a White Sox rebuild team reads as quietly useful. The question this profile hinges on is whether the spin keeps translating to weak contact in zone — if the chase rate slips and hitters start sitting on that fastball, the walk rate at 7.3% doesn't leave much runway.

reports.name: Andrés Muñoz
reports.published_report: The strikeout profile is almost absurd: 35.7% K rate, 40.8% whiff rate, a 38.2% chase rate, all sitting at the top of the sport. Muñoz generates swing-and-miss at a rate that makes contact nearly academic. The tension is the walk rate, 9.7%, sitting well below average, and it's what holds the xERA at 3.50 and the xwOBA at .290 — numbers that say "good reliever" rather than "untouchable one." If the walks tighten, the strikeout stuff elevates him into a genuine closer anchor; if 9.7% is simply who he is, the projection's 27 saves and 3.56 ERA over 58.1 innings is the ceiling, a reliever who misses bats at an elite clip but donates enough free passes to keep the bottom line ordinary.

reports.name: Chad Patrick

Patrick's whiff rate sits at 26.5% and his chase rate at 31.9%, both above the middle of the pack, which tells you hitters struggle to make clean decisions against him. But a 21.3% strikeout rate and 8.9% walk rate say those decisions aren't costing them enough — he's generating weak contact and missed swings without converting them into outs at a rate that matters. The xERA and xwOBA both land at the 50th percentile, and that's the honest ceiling here: a reliever-starter hybrid who eats innings at roughly league-average quality, worth something in a Milwaukee bullpen that needs length, but exposed the moment he's asked to be more than that. The projection's 3.61 ERA over 108.1 innings would be a pleasant surprise given the Statcast floor, and it hinges entirely on whether that barrel suppression (6.8%) holds at the volume a starter demands.

reports.name: Brooks Brannon
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 261 AA PA.
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loud number, and it's also the problem. At .314 at AA, with a .593 slugging mark that translates to roughly .200 ISO against MLB pitching, Brooks Brannon is hitting the ball over walls at a rate that almost no one in the minors matches, yet the same 261-plate-appearance sample shows 82 strikeouts against just 29 walks, and a 31% strikeout rate that translates to 30% against big-league arms, well clear of the MLB average sitting at 22%. The power is enormous and the contact profile is genuinely worrying: a first baseman with that K% and no defensive margin for error needs the raw pop to survive the zone manipulation he'll face at the next level, and a .354 BABIP suggests some of what looks like hit-tool is the ball finding gaps rather than hard contact to all fields. If the plus power travels, he's a second-division regular; if the strikeout rate clings at 30%, the floor at first base is a bench bat who only plays when the lineup needs a right-handed thump.
reports.report: Lean everyday power bat, but the miss rate keeps a bench outcome in play; the power is the reason to stay on him. Better pitching can keep the power in the dugout with empty swings. The sample covers 261 PA in Double-A, so confidence is moderate.

reports.name: Shane Drohan
reports.published_report: The chase rate is what makes the ERA believable. At 33.9%, Drohan gets hitters to chase well above the league norm, and the walk rate sits at just 6.7%, which together explain a 3.32 xERA that the projection's 3.73 ERA is essentially catching up to. The strikeout rate at 24.0% is modest enough that this isn't a swing-and-miss profile, it's a pitch-location profile, and 2430 rpm on the fastball gives him enough carry to keep hitters honest in the zone. If the chase rate regresses, the whole arrangement gets tighter fast, because he's not burying hitters with volume of whiffs. A mid-rotation floor with genuine upside if the command holds.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 239 A PA.
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Tsung-Che Cheng
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 240 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the honest edge here. Thirty-two walks in 240 AAA plate appearances translates to a 10.5% walk rate against an MLB average of 8.5%, which is a real skill and the thing that keeps his profile from being merely a glove-and-speed placeholder. The speed is loud too, 10 stolen bases already this season, and the .351 OBP at AAA reflects both. Where it gets complicated is the power: a .17 ISO at AAA softens to .142 in MLB equivalent terms, right at or just below league average, which means the offensive profile leans heavily on getting on base rather than doing damage once he does. If the walk rate travels and the contact holds, 60 strikeouts in 240 PA is a tick above comfortable at the big-league level, Cheng is a viable bench bat who can play shortstop and run; if the strikeout rate creeps and the ISO doesn't grow, the floor is organizational depth.
reports.report: He forces pitchers into the zone and takes the free pass; the line does not show a second offensive strength at the same level. The walks create an everyday path, but the present outcome is a reserve. The sample covers 240 PA in Triple-A, so confidence is high.

reports.name: Antonio Jimenez
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 45.7 AAA IP.
reports.published_report: The latest meaningful sample is from 2025, so confidence is low. There's no repeatable way to retire hitters in the line yet. The failure point is the strikeout-to-walk result, which does not support a firm starter projection. A rotation role is not supported by the current line; the floor is organizational depth or a low-leverage bullpen assignment.
